 DSCC launches intensive clean-up drive in 29 wards to prevent dengue
 Survey detects larvae in 322 houses 
 Published : 8 November 2026
 • 
 Updated : 8 November 2026, 19:10
 • 
 ENVIRONMENT
 SHARE 
 Star Online Report 
 Photo courtesy: DSCC 
 Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) has launched a special intensive clean-up drive in 29 high-risk wards identified through a survey conducted by the corporation as part of its efforts to prevent dengue.
 The drive was inaugurated at 12:30pm today at the premises of Azimpur Government Quarters by DSCC Administrator Md Abdus Salam. The programme includes special cleaning operations and mosquito control activities.
 Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source 
 Speaking at the inauguration ceremony, the administrator said the 12-day Monsoon Aedes Larvae Survey 2026 was conducted across all 75 wards of DSCC from September 27 to October 8 to assess dengue risks and identify Aedes mosquito breeding sites.
 A total of 2,250 houses were scientifically inspected during the survey. Thirty-six field workers from DSCC and the Communicable Disease Control (CDC) branch of the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) collected data using the Kobo Toolbox application.
 Based on the survey findings and an analysis of various indicators used to measure Aedes mosquito density -- including the Breteau Index (BI), House Index (HI), Container Index (CI) and Pupal Index (PI) -- 29 of DSCC's 75 wards were classified as high-risk, 28 as moderate-risk and 18 as general-risk areas.
 Aedes mosquito larvae were detected in 322 of the houses inspected. The identified larvae were immediately destroyed, and necessary larviciding activities were also carried out, a DSCC official said.
 The survey found that high-rise and semi-permanent buildings, independent houses, buildings under construction and stagnant water in vacant plots were among the major sources of Aedes mosquito breeding.
 Based on the survey findings, the special intensive clean-up drive was launched simultaneously in the 29 high-risk wards today. The programme includes intensive larviciding and adulticiding operations, destruction of mosquito breeding sites, cleaning of drains, canals and sewerage channels, and waste removal.
 Public awareness campaigns will also be conducted through loudspeaker announcements, leaflet distribution and mosques. Special cleaning and mosquito control operations will be carried out at educational institutions and religious establishments as well.
 In addition, consultation meetings and joint operations will be organised with the participation of local representatives, various institutions and relevant stakeholders. If Aedes mosquito larvae are found anywhere despite these efforts, legal action will be taken through mobile courts, the administrator said.
 Addressing the programme, DSCC administrator said, "Preventing dengue cannot be achieved through the efforts of the city corporation alone. Alongside government agencies, the responsible and active participation of every citizen is essential.
 "Everyone must keep their homes, rooftops, balconies, courtyards and workplaces clean. Water must not be allowed to accumulate anywhere. People must develop the habit of removing stagnant water and destroying potential breeding sites at least once a week."
 He further said the survey found that 14.21 percent of the larvae were in plastic buckets, 11.22 percent in plastic drums, 9.98 percent in stagnant water in basements, 9.23 percent in plastic mugs and 5.99 percent in flower pots.
 "This means that if citizens remain vigilant about their courtyards and water-holding containers, nearly half (50.9 percent) of Aedes mosquito breeding and the associated risk of dengue can be prevented at the initial stage," he added.
